title: The torsion bound on an arbitrary algebraic curve
statement:
Let $X$ be a
separated finite-type
scheme of dimension at most one over an algebraically closed
field. Put $e=1$ if $X$ is affine, and $e=2$ otherwise.
Then $\operatorname{cd}_{\rm tor}(X)\leq e$, in the sense of
[def-sc-etale-torsion-cd].

proof.text: The reduction map $X_{\mathrm{red}}\to X$ is a universal homeomorphism: after any base change the extended ideal is generated by nilpotent elements and hence lies in every prime, so the closed immersion is a homeomorphism. By [thm-weil-pbc-universal-homeomorphism-invariance] it preserves cohomology and the local torsion condition (the equivalence preserves sections, covers, and multiplication by integers); a reduction of an affine scheme is affine. We may thus assume $X$ reduced (if the original $e=2$, any bound at most two suffices). By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] and [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components], $X$ is Noetherian with finitely many irreducible components $C_i$, given their reduced structures. Each $C_i$ is integral of finite type over $k$. Normalize $C_i$ in its own function field and set $X'=\coprod_i C_i^\nu$ and $h:X'\to X$. By [lem-fin-normalization-extension-finite] each normalization is finite; composition with the closed immersion $C_i\to X$ and the finite disjoint union are finite, as is checked by taking the finite product of their finite algebras on an affine open. On each $C_i$ choose a finite affine cover. On each affine, the finitely many generators of its normalization lie in the fraction field, so inverting a common nonzero denominator makes normalization the identity. The union of these opens is dense in $C_i$ and its closed complement is proper. Remove these complements and all intersections $C_i\cap C_j$ for $i\ne j$. Each removed subset is proper in its component and has dimension at most zero: a chain of length one in it, followed by $C_i$, would contradict $\dim X\le1$. Their finite union $S$ is closed of dimension at most zero, hence is a finite set of closed points by [lem-sc-dim0-finite]. On $U=X\setminus S$, exactly one component occurs locally and normalization is the identity, so $h^{-1}U\to U$ is an isomorphism.

The algebraically closed ground field $k$ is perfect. For each component $C_i$ of dimension one, [lem-sc-normalized-curve-smooth] applies directly to the integral finite-type $k$-scheme $C_i$, and gives that $C_i^\nu$ is smooth. By [lem-sc-normalization-exists] its dimension is one. A zero-dimensional integral $C_i$ has just its generic point, which is closed; any affine neighbourhood is the whole scheme and is the spectrum of a field. By [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a) this field is finite over $k$, hence equals $k$, and its normalization is itself. Each one-dimensional $C_i^\nu$ is integral (its affine rings are subrings of the function field), hence connected, and of finite type over $k$ (a finite algebra over a finitely generated $k$-algebra is finitely generated). It is separated: over an affine open of $X$, the diagonal of a finite morphism is the closed immersion given by the surjection $B\otimes_A B\to B$, $b\otimes c\mapsto bc$; its composite with the base change of the closed diagonal of $X/k$ is the diagonal over $k$. If $X$ is affine then $X'$ is affine because finite morphisms are affine by [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]; its finitely many open-and-closed components are affine as well.

Let $F$ be an arbitrary torsion abelian sheaf on the small etale site of $X$, with torsion understood exactly as in the current [def-sc-etale-torsion-cd]: each local section is locally annihilated by a positive integer. No uniform annihilator of $F$ or torsion hypothesis on every section group is assumed. All cohomology below is ordinary derived-section cohomology, as in that definition. The adjunction unit $\varphi:F\to h_*h^*F$ restricts to an isomorphism on $U$: for an etale $V\to U$, its inverse image under $h$ is $V$, so the unit is the identity on its sections. Every point of $S$ has residue field $k$ by [lem-kun-closed-point-field](a), hence separably closed. Therefore [lem-sc-iso-off-finite-set-cohomology] gives $H^q(X,F)\cong H^q(X,h_*h^*F)$ for $q\ge2$. By [lemma-weil-pbc-finite-direct-image-exact], $Rh_*=h_*$; composing derived sections with $Rh_*$ gives $H^q(X,h_*h^*F)\cong H^q(X',h^*F)$. The pullback is torsion: by [lem-weil-pbc-inverse-image-stalk-germ] its geometric stalks are stalks of $F$, which are torsion by [lem-weil-pbc-torsion-sheaf-characterizations], and the converse in that characterization applies to $h^*F$. On each smooth connected one-dimensional component use [lem-sc-cohomological-dimension] for $q>2$, or [lem-sc-affine-cohomological-dimension] for $q>1$ if the original $X$ was affine. On each point use [lem-weil-pbc-zero-dimensional-cohomology]. Sections on a finite disjoint union are the finite product of the component section functors, and this finite product is exact, so the same componentwise decomposition holds for their derived functors. Consequently $H^q(X',h^*F)=0$ for every $q>e$. Since $q>e\ge1$ implies $q\ge2$, the comparison proves the required bound, including the empty scheme (the empty product of groups is zero). Since $F$ was arbitrary with this local torsion condition, this vanishing is precisely $\operatorname{cd}_{\rm tor}(X)\leq e$ by [def-sc-etale-torsion-cd]. The two smooth-curve statements apply to any torsion sheaf, without a uniform-annihilator hypothesis; the finite-support comparison and finite direct-image exactness apply even to arbitrary abelian sheaves.
